Question
========
Draw a proper graph that approximates the latency of a web server about 100 km away from you, as a function of the number of concurrent requests.

Think about what the latency of a web server is when you actually browse the web. The graph should follow all the standards seen about data visualization.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6.6, fig.height=5.0}
par(mar=c(0,0,0,0)); plot.new(); plot.window(c(0,100),c(0,100))
rect(1,1,99,99)
arrows(12,10,94,10,length=.1); arrows(12,10,12,92,length=.1)
text(53,5,"Concurrent requests",cex=.8); text(6,50,"Latency (ms)",srt=90,cex=.8)
```

Solution
========
The curve is flat then hockey sticks. At low concurrency the latency is dominated by the round trip: 100 km of fibre is about 1 ms of propagation there and back, and a real server answers in a few milliseconds, so the floor sits around 5 to 20 ms. That floor does not depend on the load.

As concurrency grows the server approaches saturation, queueing appears and the latency climbs steeply, reaching hundreds of milliseconds and then growing without bound once the arrival rate exceeds the service rate.

Expected of the graph: both axes labelled with units, a Y axis that starts at zero or is explicitly logarithmic, an X range covering enough concurrency to show the knee, and ideally the knee annotated. A flat line or a straight increasing line are both wrong.
